rule.name: World and Count
rule.text: The suit picks a world: Spades is the sea, Hearts is the kitchen, Diamonds is the market and Clubs is the forest. The rank picks the picture: an Ace is one big thing from that world, a number card shows that many of something (two oars, five arms, ten fish), and Jack, Queen and King are always people of that world, the young helper, the expert and the chief. Learn one world and you already know a quarter of the deck.
plan: Day 1: learn the Spades world (13 pictures). Say each card code and its picture aloud, then cover the list and test yourself.
Day 2: Hearts. Day 3: Diamonds. Day 4: Clubs. Take a day off whenever a world still feels wobbly.
Then shuffle and flip single cards, saying the picture within two seconds. Only start Deck Run once you can do that for most of the deck.

own: These are suggestions. If a picture does not work for you, swap it for one that does, and keep the same rule so you can rebuild it. A picture you chose yourself is stronger than one you were handed. The game does not save your own card pictures in 1.1; keep them on paper.
codes: Card code is rank then suit letter: AS is Ace of Spades, 10H is Ten of Hearts, KC is King of Clubs. S is Spades, H is Hearts, D is Diamonds, C is Clubs. Suits are never shown by colour alone (the Cards drill draws each suit as shape and letter).

guide.title: How to lay a deck along a route
steps: Pick a route you know well with 13 to 26 stops (a palace, a street or a commute). You need half as many stops as cards, because each stop holds two cards.
Flip the cards two at a time. Turn both into pictures from your card list. Let the first picture do something to the second at the stop, such as pushing, pouring, eating or weighing it.
Move to the next stop for the next two cards. Keep the action short and a little silly. Do not stop to fix a picture that is a bit weak.
At recall, walk the route from stop 1, say the two cards at each stop and place them in order. If a stop is blank, leave a gap and keep going rather than guess.
Check against the deck. Look for the pattern of your errors (a mixed-up suit, a swapped pair) and fix that, not everything.

stops.scene: A big maple leaf with five points is weighed on a two-pan scale, and the scale tips right over the doormat.
Nine pearls spill from an oyster onto a four-legged kitchen table that is reflected in the mirror.

guide.honestNote: Memorising the order of a shuffled deck is a memory sport. It trains turning a card into a picture and placing pictures along a route, and it does not carry much into daily life. Cards in Mnemos give no skill points and no Lumen. They are here for people who want the challenge, and you can skip them with no cost to your year.

ladder.note: Roughly six seconds a card to study. Finishing early is allowed and the time is recorded. A personal best counts only when the deck is longer, or the time shorter at the same length and accuracy.

deckRun.realFormatInOurWords: Real memory contests include a shuffled-deck event in which a deck is memorised and then recalled in order. Rules and timing differ between contests, so none is described.
deckRun.ourVersion: 10 to 52 cards from the ladder. Study the cards a row of four at a time. Recall by tapping cards into numbered slots, with undo, or typing codes such as 10H. Two trials, the better one counts.
deckRun.scoring: Score is the longest correct run from card 1. Accuracy (right positions over cards) is shown too, for information. No Lumen, no skill points.
advice: Move at a steady pace. Rushing a hard deck gives you a short run.
Fix weak pictures before you add speed.
Practise the shortest deck you can do perfectly, then add 5 cards.

doubleDeck.realFormatInOurWords: Real memory contests include card events with more than one deck. Names and rules differ between contests, so none is described.
doubleDeck.ourVersion: One order of 26 to 52 cards, asked by position in random order (for example: what is card number 17?). Seconds per answer are off by default, and a short pace switch is optional. One miss ends the round gently, with the answers shown.
doubleDeck.scoring: Score is the number of correct answers before the first miss. No Lumen, no skill points. The Echo scene version uses resolve 3, as the plan sets for the three elimination scenes, while the plain drill ends at the first miss.
advice: Practise answering from any position, not only walking the route in order.
Know where each stop starts: number stops 1 to 26 so you can jump straight to stop 9.
Use the break to rehearse the first and last stops.

dayPlan.title: A four-week way in (suggested)
weeks: Week 1: learn the four worlds, one a day.
Week 2: flip single cards and say the pictures fast. Then 10 card runs, two per stop.
Week 3: 15 and 20 card runs. Check your error pattern each time.
Week 4: 26 cards. Try Double Deck on a 26 card order. Rest a day, then try a longer deck.

plain.intro: Cards are a sport inside the Event Hall. You turn each card into a picture, place pairs of pictures along a route and rebuild the order. Take it slowly and enjoy the game, since cards are optional.
plain.honest: Cards train one skill: turning a card into a picture and placing it. They do not make anything else in life easier, so they give no skill points and no Lumen. They are here for the challenge.
